blocks.content: This chapter opens a new module surveying inter process communication, IPC, as a whole, the general problem of getting two separate processes to exchange information. Pipes and shared memory, both already covered in dedicated chapters in the Linux module, are two specific IPC mechanisms. Message passing is the other major conceptual family, and understanding it properly requires seeing it as a genuine alternative philosophy, not just another mechanism on the same list.

Where shared memory hands two processes the same physical pages and lets them sort out coordination themselves, message passing keeps processes fully separate and moves discrete, self contained messages between them instead, with the kernel or a runtime actively mediating every single exchange.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409506387-989633116.png
1. The Core Model: send and receive
blocks.text: 1. The Core Model: send and receive

blocks.content: Every message passing system, regardless of its specific implementation, builds on exactly two fundamental operations. send hands a complete, self contained message to the kernel or runtime, addressed to some destination. receive retrieves the next available message addressed to the calling process, or blocks until one arrives.

This is a genuinely different communication model from shared memory. There is no region of memory both sides read and write directly, every single piece of information that crosses between the two processes travels as one complete, bounded message, handled by an intermediary that neither process needs to trust the other to cooperate with correctly.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409506388-461827601.png
blocks.alt: The Core Model: send and receive

blocks.content: 2. Message Passing vs Shared Memory

The shared memory chapter was explicit about its central tradeoff: extremely fast, direct access, at the cost of providing absolutely no built in synchronization, leaving every bit of coordination entirely up to the application, with a real risk of the exact race conditions covered in the synchronization module.

Message passing takes the opposite side of this tradeoff deliberately. Because every exchange passes through a kernel or runtime mediated send and receive, there is no shared, mutable memory region for two processes to corrupt through uncoordinated concurrent access at all. The real cost is the copying and mediation overhead this safety requires, echoing the exact same copying cost the pipes chapter described for pipes specifically, since a pipe is itself one particular, restricted form of message passing.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507301-253042674.png

3. Direct vs Indirect Naming

A message passing system needs some way for a sender to specify where a message should go. Direct naming has the sender explicitly name the exact receiving process, send to process B specifically. This is simple, but it means the sender needs to know precisely which process it is talking to.

Indirect naming instead has the sender address a shared intermediary, commonly called a mailbox or a port, rather than a specific process. Any process with access to that mailbox can receive the message, decoupling the sender from needing to know exactly which process will actually handle it, which is precisely the flexibility a system like message queues, covered in the next chapter, is built around.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507302-954097481.png
4. Synchronous vs Asynchronous Communication

A second independent design choice is whether send blocks the sender until the message has actually been received. Synchronous, blocking message passing has the sender pause until a receiver actually takes the message, sometimes called a rendezvous, giving both sides a guaranteed, precise handoff moment with no ambiguity about timing.

Asynchronous, non blocking message passing instead lets the sender continue immediately after handing off a message, without waiting for it to actually be received. This requires somewhere to hold messages that have been sent but not yet received, a buffer, introducing the capacity question covered next.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507302-694768431.png
5. Buffer Capacity: Zero, Bounded, or Unbounded
blocks.text: 5. Buffer Capacity: Zero, Bounded, or Unbounded

blocks.content: When communication is asynchronous, the size of the buffer holding undelivered messages becomes a real, practical design decision with genuine consequences, directly echoing the blocking behavior already covered in the pipes chapter for exactly this reason.

blocks.title: A direct echo of the pipes chapter
blocks.content: A pipe kernel buffer filling up and blocking its writer is a concrete, real world instance of exactly this bounded capacity behavior, message passing theory and the pipes chapter mechanics describe the same underlying tradeoff from two different angles.
6. The Message Passing Family, Surveyed

Message passing is not one single mechanism, it is a conceptual family several concrete, real world mechanisms belong to, each making its own specific choices along the naming, synchrony, and capacity dimensions just covered.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507303-731388812.png
7. Why Message Passing Is Sometimes the Only Option
blocks.text: 7. Why Message Passing Is Sometimes the Only Option

blocks.content: Shared memory fundamentally requires both communicating processes to be running on the same physical machine, sharing the same physical RAM. The instant two processes need to communicate across a network, on genuinely separate machines, shared memory is not merely slower, it is not possible at all, there is no shared physical memory to map into both address spaces.
/engineering/library/os/images/1785409507303-866279053.png
blocks.alt: Why Message Passing Is Sometimes the Only Option

blocks.content: Message passing has no such restriction. Since it never required directly shared physical memory in the first place, the exact same conceptual model, send and receive, extends naturally across a network, which is precisely why sockets, covered later in this module, are built on message passing principles rather than shared memory ones.
8. Common Mistakes and Interview Angle

["Treating message passing as strictly slower and therefore strictly worse than shared memory in every case, when it is the only viable option at all once processes are no longer on the same machine.","Assuming every message passing system is synchronous by default, when asynchronous, buffered message passing is extremely common and has its own real capacity tradeoffs to reason about.","Confusing direct naming with indirect naming, and not recognizing that indirect naming, through a mailbox or port, is specifically what decouples a sender from needing to know exactly which process will handle a message."]
items: Treating message passing as strictly slower and therefore strictly worse than shared memory in every case, when it is the only viable option at all once processes are no longer on the same machine.
Assuming every message passing system is synchronous by default, when asynchronous, buffered message passing is extremely common and has its own real capacity tradeoffs to reason about.

Confusing direct naming with indirect naming, and not recognizing that indirect naming, through a mailbox or port, is specifically what decouples a sender from needing to know exactly which process will handle a message.

blocks.title: Interview angle
blocks.content: Be ready to explain the fundamental tradeoff between shared memory and message passing precisely, and to explain why message passing, unlike shared memory, generalizes naturally to communication across a network, not just within a single machine.

With the general message passing model established, the rest of this module works through its concrete, real world implementations: message queues next, followed by sockets, and finally a fresh look at pipes and signals specifically through the IPC lens this module has now introduced.
